segments.text: Park a Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II next to a brand-new Boeing F-15EX Eagle II on a U.S. Air Force runway and ask one question.
Which fighter belongs to the future of war?
On enemy radar, the stealthy F-35A shrinks to the size of a metal golf ball, hiding its weapons inside sealed belly bays.
Beside it towers the F-15EX, a twin-tailed giant whose silhouette dates back to 1972.

With zero stealth shaping, it hangs missiles, bombs, and fuel tanks out in the open wind, lighting up Russian or Chinese radar with a cross-section exceeding 100 to 200 square feet, about as subtle as a flying semi-truck.
Now guess which jet costs the Pentagon more to buy.
Mass production puts an F-35A's flyaway price around $82 million to $92 million.
Recent F-15EX deals, including the Lot 7 contract awarded in September 2026, price each airframe between $97 million and $108 million, before adding the engines.
Stranger still, with 120 jets under contract, the Air Force moved in its fiscal 2027 budget request to more than double the planned fleet to 267 aircraft.
Paying over $100 million a piece for a non-stealthy 1970s design sounds insane, until you peel off its gray skin.
Underneath hides a flying supercomputer, an electronic force field, a 50-year wingtip secret, and nearly 15 tons of firepower built for the brutal jobs stealth fighters physically cannot touch.
To see why engineers rebuilt the Eagle from the bones out, rewind to November 2, 2007, 18,000 feet above Missouri.
During training, an Air National Guard pilot banked his F-15C Eagle into a routine 450-knot, 7.8G turn.
Suddenly, a gunshot crack tore through the frame.
Right behind the cockpit, the fighter snapped in half in midair.
The nose ripped free and tumbled as the pilot ejected, surviving with a broken shoulder.
Investigators traced the failure to an upper-right fuselage beam called a longeron.
Machined fractions of an inch too thin in the early 1980s, it had grown fatigue cracks over thousands of dogfights until it snapped.
The crash grounded older Eagles worldwide and exposed a ticking clock.
Cold War F-15s, built for 4,000 to 8,000 flight hours, were wearing out.
Surprisingly, U.S. taxpayers didn't fund the redesign from scratch.
During the 2010s, Saudi Arabia and Qatar poured roughly $5 billion into Boeing's St. Louis plant to develop modernized export models, the F-15SA and F-15QA.
When the Pentagon needed an urgent replacement for aging F-15Cs and eventually overworked F-15E strike eagles,
that heavy structural engineering was already paid for.
Strip the aluminum and titanium skin off an F-15EX and you meet an all-new skeleton.
Using 3D digital full-size determinant assembly, Boeing mills monolithic wing ribs, reinforced longerons,
and alloy bulkheads with pre-aligned holes that lock together with microscopic precision.
While an F-35A airframe is rated for 8,000 flight hours, the F-15EX is certified for 20,000 flight hours, built to pull high-G turns into the 2060s.
That skeleton preserves the Eagle's greatest aerodynamic trick.
Its wide, flat center fuselage acts as a giant lifting body.
In 1983, an Israeli F-15D lost nearly its entire right wing in a mid-air collision, leaving just a jagged two-foot stump.
Lighting the afterburners, the wide torso generated enough lift to touch down at 260 knots, nearly 300 miles per hour, stopping 20 feet short of the runway barrier.
Inside the F-15EX, Boeing didn't just strengthen the bones.
They ripped out its mechanical nervous system, unlocking two forbidden missile stations dormant on Eagle wings for half a century.
Look under any legacy U.S.
And you'll spot unused hardpoints near the outer wingtips.
Station 1 on the left, and Station 9 on the right.
Every Eagle since the 1970s had provisions for them.
Yet early tests uncovered a deadly trap.
Hanging heavy stores near those swept wingtips triggered violent aero-elastic flutter, a high-speed twisting vibration capable of tearing the wings off.
Legacy Eagles ran on steel cables, pulleys, pushrods, and hydraulic valves that couldn't counter those vibrations fast enough.
For nearly 50 years, Stations 1 and 9 stayed sealed shut.
Inside the F-15EX, mechanical cables give way to quad-redundant digital fly-by-wire.
Moving the stick sends electrical votes to four flight computers sampling air loads and wing flex hundreds of times per second,
flicking control surfaces by fractions of an inch to kill flutter before the pilot feels a tremor.
On November 29, 2022, over the Gulf of Mexico out of Eglin Air Force Base, 96th test wing pilots proved it live,
firing an AIM-120 AMRAAM from Station 1 and an AIM-9X Sidewinder from Station 9.
Unlocking those tips boosts the Evil-2's standard air-to-air load from 8 missiles to 12,
triple what an F-35A carries internally today.
Push its 23 weapon stations further with proposed amber multi-ejector racks,
and one F-15EX could conceptually haul up to 22 air-to-air missiles,
plus 500 rounds for the 20mm M61A1 Vulcan 6-barrel cannon in its right wing route.
Yet small missiles aren't even the main reason stealth jets need this machine.
Look beneath the center belly pylon.
Stealth lives inside a geometric prison.
To stay invisible, weapons must fit inside internal bays sized around 12-foot missiles.
Hang oversized ordnance under an F-35's wings, and stealth vanishes.
Rated for an Air Force record 29,500 pounds of payload, nearly 15 tons,
the F-15EX features a reinforced centerline pylon engineered for a single outsized weapon up to 22 feet long and weighing 7,000 pounds.
Hypersonic strike missiles and giant bunker busters that could never fit inside an F-22 or F-35 ride effortlessly under an Eagle II.
Hauling 15 tons of ordnance, plus 13,500 pounds, roughly 2,000 gallons,
of internal fuel pushes maximum takeoff weight to 81,000 pounds.
Hurling over 40 tons of metal past twice the speed of sound takes raw violence.
Slide back into the tailpipes to meet twin General Electric F-110 GE-129 afterburning turbofans.
Governed by digital engine controls, each blasts out over 29,000 pounds of thrust, more than 58,000 pounds combined.
In air superiority trim, those turbines produce more thrust than the airplane weighs.
Departing Street
Lewis, test pilots show off that power with the Viking takeoff.
Seconds after wheels up, the pilot pulls nearly 90 degrees straight vertical, rocketing past 30,000 feet in under a minute.
Above 45,000 feet, the F-15EX hits Mach 2.5, over 1,650 miles per hour,
outpacing both the Mach 1.6 F-35A and the Mach 2.25 F-22 Raptor.
Why does Mach 2.5 matter against Mach 4 missiles?
Launch physics
Releasing an AMRAAM or a 7,000-pound hypersonic booster at Mach 2-plus and 50,000 feet
turns the fighter into a reusable first-stage rocket, slingshotting U.S.
Weapons miles farther than slower jets can shoot,
while letting the Eagle II whip around and outrun the outer fuel burn of enemy missiles.
Still, speed won't save you when hostile radar spots a 200-square-foot target from 150 miles out.
Without stealth skin, how does the F-15EX survive contested scotties?
Instead of hiding in the dark, it blinds everyone looking at it.
Inside the wide nose cone sits Raytheon's liquid-cooled AN-APG-82-V1-AESA radar.
Using F-22-derived processing, its solid-state array steers thousands of radio beams in microseconds,
tracking air and surface targets simultaneously.
Fiber-optic lines feed that data into Honeywell's ADCP-2 mission computer,
crunching 87 billion instructions per second,
the fastest core supercomputer ever put in a tactical fighter.
That brain drives BAE Systems' AN-ALQ-250E PAWSS electronic warfare suite
across fuselage antennas and twin tail-top pods.
For decades, electronic warfare faced a self-blinding trap.
Turning on powerful radar jammers drowned out a fighter's own nose radar,
forcing older jets to blink jammers off just to see.
Inside the F-15EX, tunable radio frequency filters and co-site mitigation
slice out microscopic frequency windows in real time.
EPA-WSS blasts deceptive digital noise,
flooding enemy screens with phantom targets and false range data
at the exact microsecond the APG-82 radar holds an unbroken lock on the shooter.
Against heat seekers, four added tail dispensers boost capacity by 50%,
packing 360 chaff and flare cartridges across 12 AN-ALE-47 housings.
Climb into the canopy, though, and you spot a multi-million dollar mystery.
Analog dials give way to a 10x19-inch HD touchscreen large area display,
a low-profile digital HUD, an ACES-5 smart ejection seat,
and the JH MCS-2 helmet visor that locks missiles wherever the pilot looks.
Now glance behind the pilot.
Every F-15EX is built with two seats, rear controls, and a second 10x19-inch touchscreen.
Yet, since achieving initial operational capability in July 2024 with Oregon's 142nd wing in Portland,
air superiority units fly solo, leaving that back seat completely empty.
Why haul an empty cockpit?
Built on open mission systems architecture,
the F-15EX plugs in new weapons and software like smartphone apps for tomorrow's battles.
Picture a Pacific clash, where 36 F-15EXs are slated for Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan,
following the August 2026 rollout of the first Kadena-coded jet.
Ahead, stealthy F-35As slip silently inside enemy air defense rings,
spotting targets passively without exposing their four missile bays.
60 miles back prowls a flight of F-15EXs, now carrying a weapon systems officer in back.
Over-encrypted data links, F-35s pass target coordinates backward,
and the Eagle IIs unleash salvos of AMRAAMs or hypersonic missiles from standoff safety.
Simultaneously, on that rear touchscreen,
the backseater quarterback's unmanned collaborative combat aircraft,
loyal wingman, drones scouting radar traps and drawing enemy fire miles ahead.
Does that guarantee the Eagle's undefeated 104-0 air-to-air kill record survives?
Not automatically. Pentagon reports exposed three sharp vulnerabilities.
First is the missing fuel tank catch. Early test jets wore side-mounted conformal fuel tanks
holding roughly 1,500 extra gallons, over 10,000 pounds of low-drag fuel, plus extra bomb racks.
To cut upfront costs and prioritize air defense, the Air Force fielded initial operational units
without them. Pentagon testers warned that skipping conformal tanks reduces unrefueled range,
forces draggy wing-drop tanks onto weapon pylons,
and leaves early squadrons with minimal precision ground strike capability until later lots add them.
Second, government accountability office audits revealed Boeing misdrilled windscreen holes
on four Lot-1B jets due to faulty tooling, followed by supplier bottlenecks and a late 2025 strike
that delayed deliveries by months.
Third, electronic warfare cannot repeal physics.
Adversary missiles increasingly pair AESA radar seekers with imaging infrared sensors
and passive home-on-jam modes tracking a jammer's own beam.
If the stealth screen breaks and an F-15EX gets ambushed close to modern air defenses,
200 square feet of roaring metal has nowhere to hide.
Yet, pitting the F-15EX against stealth misses the entire point.
You don't use a scalpel to smash a concrete wall, and you don't swing a sledgehammer for surgery.
Stealth fighters slip through the dark to unlock the door.
Then, thundering behind them at Mach 2.5 with a 20,000-hour skeleton,
unlocked wingtips, 87 billion calculations a second,
and 15 tons of fury under its wings,
the F-15EX Eagle II tears the entire building down.
